subject: cardboardRobot
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: kid in a cardboard-box robot costume.
Style: cardboard craft.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a cardboard-box robot costume design for a young kid, focusing on authentic craft details like corrugated textures, tape, foil, bottle caps, straws, and googly eyes to keep it feeling handmade.

For the rig, I'm working out a humanoid structure with a torso box, a helmet box with a face cutout revealing the kid's face, foil-wrapped tube arms, and cardboard-box shin pieces over jeans with sneakers, then starting to define the body proportions and vertical positioning from the feet up.

I'm settling on an A-pose for the arms, angled out and down diagonally from the shoulders with separate upper arm and forearm segments. For hands, I'm debating simple gloved hands with fingers versus cute foil claw hands like a cardboard robot's lobster mitts.

Now I'm defining the leg skeleton with hip, knee, and ankle joints for straight standing legs, building each finger as a two-joint chain so the digits read as separate.

Still defining the spine chain...

With one name and one span, there's no tip joint, which works fine for a two-point polyline. I'm thinking the kid's neck is mostly hidden between the torso box and helmet, so I could use the open cardboard flaps at the top of the box as a nice visual detail framing the neck opening.

Visible kid parts would be face, neck, hands, legs, and shoes, with arms exiting through side holes wearing a striped sleeve. I'm considering foil-wrapped cardboard tube segments as robot-arm armor over the sleeves, maybe pairing a rigid tube upper arm with an accordion dryer-hose forearm for the costume effect.

Now I'm working out hands as bare skin with visible fingers, forearms covered by foil tube sleeves banded with red tape, and legs in painted blue denim-textured jeans topped by boxy cardboard shin guards running from knee to ankle with foiled edges, plus sneakers to finish the look.

Sneakers will be reddish with white soles. For the torso box, I want a kraft cardboard look built from mottled brown noise textures with subtle corrugation lines on the cut edges, and I'm planning an SVG chest panel showing a control display with buttons, dials, a meter, and a handwritten marker label.

For the kid's face, I'll build the head as a sphere with skin paint and layered decals for eyes, mouth, freckles, eyebrows, and mop-style hair, framed by a helmet window cut into the box front using surrounding slab panels.

Working out the precise helmet dimensions and window placement so the head sits properly centered within the cutout, aligning the front planes so the face reads clearly through the window opening.

I also need to handle the jaw mechanism separately—since the mouth has to open, I need to build the cranium as one piece and construct the lower jaw as its own distinct geometry rather than combining them into a single solid head shape.

I'll simplify the mouth into an upper lip curve on the head and a lower lip curve on the jaw, keeping it as two manageable sweep shapes. For eyes, I'm planning to decal an SVG eye graphic—white sclera, big brown iris, highlights—onto the skull's surface using the part's geometry.

Now I'm working out precise model-space coordinates for the head center and mirrored eye positions, projecting the decal onto the surface along a forward direction to avoid axis confusion with the tilted head bone.

Mirroring isn't needed since the eyes are symmetric. I'm also reconsidering how much of the face and hair should be visible through the helmet window—maybe a full enclosed helmet hides too much character, so I'm thinking of adding a fringe of hair peeking out at the top of the window plus possibly ears poking out the sides for a more kid-like look.

I'm deciding ears are too fiddly to fit given the window and head proportions, so I'll skip them and just focus on getting a bit of hair showing through the window instead.

Now I'm working out the helmet window placement so it frames the face correctly — figuring the helmet center height, its top/bottom bounds, and sizing the window opening so eyes down to chin are visible given typical kid-face proportions.

There's only a small gap between torso top and helmet bottom, so the neck peeks out slightly — fine for a cute proportion. I'll lower the torso box to 0.54–1.02, letting it cover the hips, with legs running hip 0.55, knee 0.30, ankle 0.075, accepting slightly short legs since the torso box hides the joint.

For the collar, I'm adding four flaps around the top opening of the torso box, hinged at the neck edge and tilted outward like an open V shape, sized to leave a hole for the head to pass through.

Positioning the flaps slightly outward and downward with a modest 25-30° droop for a loose, untidy cardboard look, mirroring rotation for opposite sides using z-axis rotation in degrees, centering each flap box geometry at the hinge offset by half its length.

Working out the back flap rotation similarly, with the opposite sign so the far end lifts instead. I'm accepting some minor overlap between the front/back and side flaps at the corners since they're separate tilted planes and won't actually z-fight, then checking whether the flaps end up tall enough to occlude the helmet sitting above.

Now I'm sketching the cardboard torso as a box body with a kraft paint texture, and planning to add silver duct-tape strips along the edges for detail.

Now I'm thinking about the chest control panel: a small glued-on cardboard rectangle painted with marker colors, decorated with bottle-cap buttons in red, blue, and green, a paper-plate dial, a gauge, and a bendy pipe-cleaner wire. I'm considering adding a couple of glowing "bulb" elements for visual flair, though it's optional.

I'll skip the clockwork gauge dependency and draw my own gauge face in SVG instead, keeping things self-contained with just the glow kit for lights, and handle the foil texture with custom noise-based crinkle paint rather than an external asset. Now I'm planning the texture list, starting with the chest panel marker drawing showing sliders and a "ROBO-KID" label.

Continuing the list: eye details, the gauge dial, a cardboard-style back panel with "THIS WAY UP" arrows, fragile stamps and a barcode, hand-drawn rivets and X-marks on the knee boxes, freckle and blush decals for the cheeks, a hair fringe texture, and a helmet side drawing with ear-muff or antenna details plus bendy-straw elements on top.

Now I'm adding a speaker grille texture to the helmet side, tape strip details rendered as flat colored boxes with a painted crinkle look, and a hanging "HELLO my name is" sticker tag on the torso box. I'm settling on a cardboard-craft palette of kraft tones, dark kraft, light interior cardboard, white paper, red tape, silver foil, and marker black/blue for the overall style.

For the kid's anatomy, I'm working out warm peach skin and brown mop hair built from a skull cap plus fringe blades, figuring out exactly which portion of the fringe peeks through the helmet's front window given the overlapping geometry between the window opening and the helmet's top bar.

I'm checking whether the hair cap sphere sits behind the skull surface at forehead height so it doesn't poke through the face, comparing radii at the eye line to make sure hair stays tucked above the eyes.

Placing brows as small curved capsules just below the hairline, with a small nose sphere, mouth position, and blush/freckle details on the cheeks. Now I'm working out the jaw geometry as a separate lower-front piece hinging down toward the chin, positioned beneath the main skull sphere.

For the mouth, I'm defining upper and lower lip lines at the skull-jaw junction with a darker recessed strip for the mouth opening, then sketching a smile curve across the face surface using a function to compute the depth at each point along the curve.

Better idea: cast rays against the skull and jaw surfaces directly to get accurate hit points with normals, then offset slightly outward and sweep curves through them—upper lip following skull-only hits (bound to head), lower lip following jaw-only hits—using separate lip-colored sweeps for each, plus a darker interior for the mouth cavity.

I'll place the mouth decal across the skull and jaw with teeth included, then add cheek decals with freckles and blush on each side, confirming the decal targeting works with surface arrays. I should also check whether ears would poke through the helmet's side bars given the head's width at that point.

Deciding to skip ears since they'd clip into the bar's inner face, I'll move on to sketching the helmet's panel layout: a top slab, side and back slabs, and front bars sized to the helmet's overall box dimensions, built as thin cardboard-thickness panels.

For finishing touches, I'm adding tape at the corner edges and bendy-straw antennae on each side of the helmet, curving upward with a bend and tipped with a glowing foil ball, using striped paint along the straw's axis. I'm also working out how to fake a coil/spring shape using a spiral helper function, reasoning through how its center and starting point parameters relate to the axis.

Then I settle on a coiled green spring antenna with a ping-pong ball tip on one side and a bendy straw with a glowing red-LED foil ball on the other. I also add toilet-paper-roll "speaker" tubes on each side of the helmet with foil end-discs textured with concentric rings, positioning them near the helmet's side center.

Now I'm working out the helmet geometry precisely: side walls spanning the full depth, front plate bars with specific thickness and position for the window, and placing the speaker tubes along the x-axis with a small radius and length.

For decoration, I'm adding some playful details to the helmet front—maybe a few colored caps resembling LEDs on the top bar, and considering a hazard-stripe tape band across the front using a striped paint pattern for visual flair.

Now shifting to the torso box: I'm planning a front panel centered on the chest, painted in a blue-gray cardboard tone with marker-drawn details like white and yellow lines and labeled sliders, positioned appropriately below the neck/head area within the torso's height range.

I'm laying out tape strips along the top and bottom seams of the panel area, then placing a round gauge dial off-center, a trio of bottle-cap knobs along the bottom, and slider marks plus LED bulbs on the opposite side to balance the composition.

Now I'm adding a raised red push button near the panel center and sketching curved pipe-cleaner-style wires that sweep across the box's front face from the panel to a hole, lifted slightly off the surface for a dimensional look.

For the arm attachment, I'm working out hole placement on the side faces for shoulder joints, positioning the upper arm segments starting at the shoulder point and extending outward to the elbow.

Building the arm chain as a sweep through shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints, with sleeve stripes rendered along the upper section and a separate foil-tube overlay covering the forearm for a smoother bent silhouette.

Adding tape ring accents at wrist and elbow using short tube sweeps, then moving on to hand geometry with a palm box and fingers oriented along the forearm's straight-arm direction.

Defining finger joint positions...

Finishing the thumb path and checking total joint counts stay well under budget across arms and legs. For legs I'm laying out hip-knee-ankle chains with tapering thigh-to-ankle radii, and planning denim-style mottled paint for the jeans with the torso box overlapping the upper leg slightly.

Now I'm adding cardboard shin boxes around the lower legs, tapering their width down toward the ankle and positioning them against the knee joint as a rigid bone, plus considering foil accents at the top rim to suggest knee pads.

Then I'm adding rivets with circles, an arrow, and a zigzag decal, checking that the shin box fits within the leg spacing. For the sneakers, I'm sketching a swept shape from heel to toe using a chain of points with elliptical cross-sections to form a simple high-top sneaker.

I'm settling on four named joints per leg chain (hip, knee, ankle, toe) so the foot's tip bone sits at the toe end, treating the ankle as the actual foot bone for rigid skinning.

Now I'm calculating the jeans sweep range by summing the thigh, shin, and foot segment lengths to figure out the parametric t-value at the ankle, then planning to use the chain's span helper to get the correct sweep boundaries instead of hardcoding them. I'm also thinking through how to attach the sneaker geometry as a loft or shape parented to the ankle joint.

Writing sneaker geometry...

Finishing the sole outline points with smoothing and thickness, then building the sneaker upper as a red ellipsoid with a white toe cap, laces as small boxes, and an ankle cuff connecting to the leg's sock area.

I'm defining a color paint function for the leg that switches between white sock and denim jeans based on the y-coordinate, keeping the ankle region white below a cutoff and jeans above it.

Next I'm sketching the neck as a short sweep chain from the spine to the head, giving it skin-colored tube geometry, and thinking about adding a striped shirt collar as a ring around the neck base.

I'm also sketching the spine chain itself, running from the hips up through two intermediate joints to the chest, and considering whether it should share a joint location with the hips or branch off cleanly.

Then I'm chaining the neck off the chest joint, attaching arms at the shoulders offset from chest, and legs off the hips, while assigning role labels like "spine", "neck", "head", "jaw", "arm", "leg", and "digit" to keep everything organized.

Now I'm defining the kraft paint shader: a tan base color with noise-based variation for subtle lightening and darkening, plus faint corrugation streaks using a sine-based flute pattern, and I'm working out the texel density needed based on total painted surface area.

Orienting the flutes based on which face normal dominates, running horizontal on side faces and along x on top faces with a small amplitude, and adding dirt smudges near the bottom plus leftover tape residue marks.

For foil material, I'm generating crinkled cell patterns to drive shading, tinting edges darker where cell boundaries meet, and adding a cooler blue tint on upward-facing normals to suggest sky reflection. Moving on to denim next.

For denim I'm blending two blue tones with noise and a faint vertical fabric grain, reusing the sock paint below the ankle line, then for the sleeve I'm setting up red/white stripes wrapped around an arm-aligned axis instead of the default body axis.

For skin I'm keeping it simple—just a flat skin tone rather than mottling or adding cheek blush, since I'll handle any rosy variation as a separate decal texture later.

For hair I'm planning a root-to-tip countershade gradient, darker at the back and base, with the cap itself flat-colored and blades using their own hair tones. For tape, I'm thinking silver duct tape gets a fine horizontal grain with sheen, while the hazard tape uses diagonal yellow-black stripes via a custom paint function.

Still writing paint definitions...

For cardboard, I'm using a darker kraft variant for the flap undersides, and I need to tally up the flat colors later to stay under the 64-color budget, keeping in mind that paints and textures don't count. For hair, I'm planning to use card-based geometry with a tuft texture scattered across the hair cap rather than individual strands.

Placing the fringe cards along the front hairline with a downward flow direction and steep lean, then scattering more cards over the crown with flow directions varying between forward-falling and back-swept to create natural coverage and some tufts sticking upward.

Since most hair would be hidden inside the helmet, I'm deciding to keep it minimal rather than wasting detail, and dropping the idea of hair poking through a helmet hole—just a small visible fringe and cap of hair is enough. I'll also prioritize getting the face settled first: big eyes, eyebrows, nose, mouth, cheeks, and freckles before finalizing hair placement.

I'm making sure helmet bars frame the face without crossing in front of it, and double-checking the hazard tape bar near the chin sits just below without clipping. Now I'm sketching the eye design as an SVG—round white sclera, brown iris, black pupil, highlights, and an upper lash line.

Writing SVG code...

Writing mouth SVG code...

Now thinking through the chest panel: setting up its viewBox and proportions, leaving space for a separate gauge decal, and deciding where to place the "ROBO-KID" title text on the box.

For the panel decoration itself, I'm sketching a speaker grille of horizontal lines in the lower-left, three vertical slider tracks with colored knobs on the right, and considering where an "ENERGY" label should sit relative to the gauge.

Still writing SVG code...

Now I'm figuring out the coordinate mapping between the SVG panel's pixel space and the physical model, working out how the viewer's left/right orientation corresponds to the model's +X axis so the decal lines up correctly on the front face.

Now I'm laying out the full panel in svg units: the gauge, three sliders with tracks and knobs, a three-LED row, a big red push button, a grille of lines, and two bottle-cap knobs, all positioned with specific coordinates so the 3D scene can map each control back correctly.

Next I'm designing the title graphic reading "ROBO-KID 3000" in a bold outlined marker style for the box front, then planning the back label with "THIS SIDE UP" arrows, a red "FRAGILE" strip, and a barcode.

I'm also placing a "HELLO my name is" sticker on the left side face with a red top band and handwritten text, positioning it carefully so none of the graphics render mirrored on their respective faces.

Checking the back-facing case confirms the same logic holds — the orientation reads correctly from the viewer's perspective without mirroring. Now I'm thinking about adding a side marker doodle on the left side, like a hand-drawn star or lightning bolt.

I'm now moving on to other decorative details: speaker-style concentric ring textures on the helmet's tube ends, a rivet and zigzag decal for the knee pads, a leaf-shaped hair tuft SVG with highlights, eyebrow sweeps, and small foil-painted spheres for the antenna tips.

Next I'm designing a low-poly crinkled-foil look using flat shading, a cream gauge face with manually computed tick marks and a needle rendered via SVG, glowing LED spheres in red/yellow/green plus a glowing antenna tip, and a lathe-generated shallow dish ring to frame the gauge like a paper plate.

Defining the rim profile...

Now I'm setting coordinate anchors: torso front at Z0=0.17, panel front at PANEL_Z=0.194, with the gauge disc layered just in front of that. I'm also considering whether to add more playful details like a cup-based chest vent, but holding back since arm holes limit what's practical on a kid costume.

I like the idea of a cardboard-tube jetpack on the back instead — two foil-wrapped paper-towel tubes mounted at x ±0.09-0.1, y 0.80, positioned behind the torso with red tape bands, paper-cup nozzles pointing downward, and cut-card flame accents for a glowing effect. I'm placing the back label centered between the tubes so it stays visible rather than covered.

Making the tubes shorter and repositioned so the label fits between them. I'm adding side doodles like a lightning bolt sticker and a "hello" nametag, plus arms sticking out near the top. For flames, I'm using glowing orange spike cones pointing downward from the nozzles to simulate thrust.

Lowering the flames further for better grounding, and texturing them like crumpled tissue paper with orange outer and yellow inner cones for a layered glow effect. The nozzles become paper-cup frustums painted red, and I'm adding thin red tape bands around the jetpack tubes for detail.

Still adding mounting hardware...

I'll use the same oversized-band trick for the silver tape at y=1.0 and the hazard band around the helmet base, sizing it to cover the front window bar region while leaving the chin area clear, then add a silver tape strip across the helmet top.

For the arm holes, I'm planning dark disc and tan ring geometry to simulate cut fabric edges — a small dark cylinder for the hole itself and a slightly larger lighter kraft-colored cylinder behind it to form a ring, positioned at the hole centers where the arms pass through.

Shoulder alignment checks out fine. For a playful touch, maybe I should add googly eyes somewhere on the costume — perhaps on an antenna ball or near the chest panel — to give the robot a fun, handmade craft feel.

I'm also thinking about adding small pipe-cleaner coils for a spring-like antenna, plus rows of little bottle-cap rivets along the box edges to simulate robot panel studs. I need to work out exact positioning so the rivets line up cleanly along the panel seams without clashing with the title text placement.

Given there's no skin deformation needed, I'll just manually loop through fixed positions and attach everything to the chest bone directly rather than dealing with the more complex callback system.

I'm assigning bones per part: torso pieces get chest, helmet pieces get head. For the head joint, I'm setting its orientation and parent in the neck chain, keeping things in model coordinates rather than local space. Then I'm adding a jaw joint positioned just below and in front of the head joint, aimed toward the lower face, with its own role and bone assignment.

For the mouth, I'm keeping the jaw closed since the decal already shows a smiling expression with teeth. The helmet attaches cleanly to the head bone so the kid's head sits properly inside it.

Now I'm working on the cardboard craft details -- adding corrugation edge strips along the flap and arm-hole edges using a striped pattern that alternates between tan and light tan colors at a fine period to mimic corrugated cardboard texture.

I've settled on about 12 texture types (eye, mouth, cheek, chest, title, gauge, backlabel, sticker, doodle, shin mark, speaker, tuft), which fits within the target range, and the overall part count should stay well under a thousand. Now I'm starting to write the actual implementation code.

Setting up the builder config with a larger paint size for finer cardboard texture detail, then defining a flat color palette for kraft, dark accents, red tape, white, and black.

Building geometry helper functions...

Defining hips as the root joint, then adding a hidden pelvis sphere for the jeans silhouette before building out the spine chain with joints at increasing heights up the torso.

Now I'm adding the neck as a short chain parented to the chest, confirming that a single-span joint list works fine for naming.

Next I'm defining the head and jaw joints, parenting head to the neck's first joint with a direction vector, and jaw off head using aim targeting toward a forward point. I'm being careful to only import functions I actually use, since unused imports might trigger strict TypeScript checks.

Now I'm sweeping the neck geometry with skin-colored tubes, then adding a collar sweep over a cropped range of the chain using from/to options with flat caps for the sleeve color.

For the head, I'm placing a scaled sphere at the skull position to create an ellipsoid shape attached to the head bone, considering segment counts for smoothness versus low-poly faceting, then building a similar sphere-based jaw part attached near the hinge.

Now I'm combining skull and jaw into a single face surface, then placing eye decals near the front of the skull and checking whether the chosen coordinates actually land on or near that surface given the ellipsoid's radii.

I'm working out decal placement for the mouth and cheeks, tilting the projection direction outward for the lateral cheek spots so the blush and freckle patterns wrap naturally around the curve, then starting to define the nose as a separate small sphere part.

Writing eyebrow placement logic...

I also need to handle rays that miss the skull with a non-null assertion helper, then move to positioning the hair cap, checking that its radius clears the skull top and back without poking through the helmet.

Checking if the hair extends far enough forward to cover the eyebrow area, comparing the hair sphere's surface distance against the skull's surface at that same point — the hair comes out slightly larger, so it does cover the brow region.

Still running into collisions between hairline and brows, so I'm restructuring the vertical layout entirely: skull center at y 1.215 with ry 0.105, placing eyes center at 1.215 to keep proportions working for a kid-like face.

Working through the numbers more, I find the hair pokes outside the skull above roughly y=1.27, which pins the hairline there; checking at x=0 confirms hair and skull surfaces match right at y=1.27, with the brow sitting safely 0.014 below.

Now I'm thinking about the fringe cards covering the forehead — draping them straight down would overshoot onto the brows, so I'm shortening the fringe length and increasing the lean angle so the bangs lie closer to the scalp and only reach down to about y=1.255, just clearing the brow line.

Since the helmet top bar hides most of the hair cap above y=1.31, only the hairline band from 1.27 to 1.31 is actually visible, so I don't need to worry about cowlicks or extra tufts up top — I'll skip those and just scatter around 40 cards over the whole cap with forward flow to avoid any bald-looking gaps in shadow.

Now I'm defining the helmet geometry on the bone head: top plate, back wall, and side walls as boxes positioned around the skull bounds, with the front face offset outward to form the brim.

Working out the front visor bars and side window struts, then considering adding corner tape details and a hazard stripe for visual accents on the helmet edges.

Now I'm skipping the window rim corrugation detail and moving on to the speaker tubes, positioning a small cylinder on each side of the head aimed outward with a textured disc cap to represent the speaker grille.

Then I'm thinking through the antennae — starting with a bendy-straw shape on the right side, plotting base and bend points to give it a curved, segmented look.

For the candy-stripe paint pattern on the straw, I'm figuring out a banding scheme based on position along the tube so the red and white stripes repeat at a reasonable spacing rather than being too fine or too coarse.

For the other arm, I'm planning a green spring coil with multiple turns, topped with a white ping-pong ball tip that has a tiny glowing yellow LED detail.

Adding more hardware details...

Placing more small details now: the gauge plate position and disc geometry, then the LED cap cylinders with glowing ball lights in red/other colors positioned along the front.

I'm computing coordinates for the three status LEDs and converting their SVG positions to model space. Then I'm laying out slider tracks and small colored knob boxes (red, yellow, white) as raised 3D tabs sitting above the drawn tracks, converting their SVG x-positions to model coordinates too.

Now I'm designing bottle-cap style knobs as ridged cylinders with a small rotated white pointer on top, and planning the big red button as a glossy cylinder with a flattened ellipsoid for its shiny cap.

For the title text, I'm positioning it as a decal plane just a few millimeters off the box's front surface so it reads clearly without clipping into the cardboard geometry.

Now I realize the duct tape band near the top would overlap the front title placement, so I need to redo the vertical layout of the torso box, shifting the title lower and keeping clear separation from the tape band.

Placing a silver rivet row beneath the panel, then adding curved red and blue wire sweeps as fuzzy pipe-cleaner strands running from the panel edges down toward the red band.
